Footnotes
[A] Radical hysterectomy with bilateral pelvic lymph node dissection is the preferred treatment for International Federation of
Gynecology and Obstetrics (FIGO) stage IA2, IB1, IB2, and select IB3-IIA1 lesions when fertility preservation is not desired.(17)
Advanced-stage disease (eg, FIGO stage IIB and above) is not usually treated with hysterectomy; in the United States, advanced-stage
disease is usually treated with definitive chemoradiation.(17) Hysterectomy may be indicated in patients with recurrent disease who did
not undergo hysterectomy as primary therapy.(17) [ A in Context Link 1 ]
[B] Several studies have found that minimally invasive or laparoscopic approaches to radical hysterectomy are associated with
decreased overall survival and disease-free survival in patients with early-stage cervical cancer; therefore, open abdominal surgery may
be preferred, and a careful discussion of long-term outcomes and oncologic risks of the surgical approaches is required.(17)(18) [ B in
Context Link 1 ]
[C] A specialty consensus guideline recommends a diagnostic excisional procedure to evaluate for invasive disease in all patients with
adenocarcinoma in situ diagnosed on cervical biopsy, even when definitive hysterectomy is planned.(7) [ C in Context Link 1 ]
[D] Cervical intraepithelial neoplasia (CIN) is the term for dysplasia or atypia in cervical epithelial cells. CIN is graded as 1, 2, or 3
depending on the degree of atypia and how much of the cervical epithelium is involved. CIN-1 (also called low-grade intraepithelial
lesion or LSIL) refers to mildly atypical changes in the lower 1/3 of the epithelium and usually resolves within 6 months without
treatment. CIN-2 indicates that there are moderately atypical cells that involve up to the lower 2/3 of the epithelium. When more than
2/3 of the epithelium has dysplasia or atypical cells, it is defined as CIN-3. CIN-2 and CIN-3, which represent higher-grade dysplasia
and are also called high-grade intraepithelial lesions or HSIL, require treatment.(7)(21) [ D in Context Link 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 ]
[E] CIN-2 and CIN-3 are sometimes classified together as CIN-2,3 due to the variability in classification of CIN-2.(7)(21) [ E in Context
Link 1, 2, 3 ]
[F] Although hysterectomy is generally recommended, a repeat excisional procedure may be preferable and is an option for some
patients.(7)(21) [ F in Context Link 1 ]
[G] Ablative procedures for cervical intraepithelial neoplasia include cryotherapy or laser ablation. Excisional procedures include loop
electrocautery excision procedure and cold-knife conization.(7) [ G in Context Link 1, 2, 3 ]
[H] A specialty society guideline concludes that, while total hysterectomy for uterine cancer can be performed by any surgical approach
(open, laparoscopic, laparoscopic with robotic assistance, or vaginal), for those with suspected uterine-confined disease, a minimally
invasive (laparoscopic, laparoscopic with robotic assistance, or vaginal) approach is recommended if technically feasible (removal of
the endometrial carcinoma en bloc with avoidance of intraperitoneal morcellation and tumor fragmentation).(22) [ H in Context Link 1 ]
[I] It is recommended that a gynecologic oncologist perform the primary surgery.(8) In early-stage disease, minimally invasive
techniques (laparoscopic with or without robotic assistance) may be considered in selected patients, if performed by an experienced
gynecologic oncologist.(8) [ I in Context Link 1 ]
[J] Recurrence of endometriosis after uterine-sparing surgical treatment may be as high as 74% with a median time to recurrence of 20
months. Hysterectomy is a reasonable initial surgical treatment choice if fertility preservation is not desired.(28) [ J in Context Link 1 ]
[K] Although a definitive diagnosis requires confirmatory histology on a biopsy specimen (eg, after hysterectomy), in clinical practice,
findings on transvaginal ultrasound or MRI are sufficient to make a provisional, actionable diagnosis, as hysteroscopy with biopsy is not
reliable because adenomyosis is not visible on hysteroscopy in most patients.(31) [ K in Context Link 1 ]
[L] If prophylactic hysterectomy is performed for PTEN hamartoma tumor syndrome, concomitant oophorectomy is not recommended
because there is no increased risk of ovarian cancer.(12) [ L in Context Link 1 ]
[M] A specialty society notes that, due to a lack of comparative effectiveness data for leiomyoma management options, a patient-
centered shared decision-making approach should be used when devising a management strategy, with counseling on all treatment
options that are available and accessible and with a discussion of the risks and benefits of various treatment options.(38)(39) [ M in
Context Link 1, 2 ]
[N] Hysterectomy may be performed coincident with pelvic organ prolapse repair.(11)(41)(42) [ N in Context Link 1 ]
[O] Validated questionnaires to assess symptoms due to pelvic organ prolapse include the Pelvic Floor Distress Inventory (PFDI), Pelvic
Floor Impact Questionnaire (PFIQ), Pelvic Organ Prolapse/Urinary Incontinence Sexual Questionnaire (PISQ-IR), and the International
Consultation on Incontinence Questionnaire-Vaginal Symptoms (ICIQ-VS).(11) [ O in Context Link 1, 2 ]
[P] Primary dysmenorrhea is a diagnosis of exclusion, after secondary causes (eg, endometriosis) of dysmenorrhea have been
excluded.(44) [ P in Context Link 1, 2 ]
[Q] Trachelectomy is the removal of the majority of the cervix and parametrial tissue up to the uterine isthmus, with preservation of the
uterus corpus.(17)(59) [ Q in Context Link 1, 2 ]
[R] See Clinical Indications for Procedure in this guideline. [ R in Context Link 1 ]
[S] Use Multimodal analgesia or individual analgesic agent as indicated. [ S in Context Link 1 ]
[T] Some patients may have their hydration needs met via alternative means (eg, percutaneous endoscopic gastrostomy tube). [ T in
Context Link 1 ]
[U] Discharge instructions should be given in the patient's and caregiver's native language using trained language interpreters
whenever possible.(73) [ U in Context Link 1 ]
Definitions
Adult Readmission Risk Assessment
Risk of readmission is increased by presence (upon admission or during hospital stay) of 1 or more of the following(1):
Acute kidney injury (ie, rise in serum creatinine 2 or more times baseline value within past 7 days)(1)
Clinically significant comorbid illness that necessitates (during current hospital stay) new or intensified treatment, prolongs
length of stay, or impacts discharge level of care (eg, heart failure, COPD, active malignancy, cirrhosis, dementia, psychosis)(1)(2)
(3)
Infection complicated by bacteremia or hypotension(1)
Need for parenteral nutrition or supplemental enteral tube feeding (eg, via gastrostomy tube or jejunostomy tube)(1)
Need for transfusion of platelets or red blood cells(1)
New need for dialysis(1)
Potential barriers to postdischarge clinical care (eg, homelessness, lack of transportation, impaired access to care or
medication, active substance abuse)(1)
Frailty (ie, as indicated by a frailty measurement tool)[A][B](1)(4)(5)(6)
Two or more emergency department visits and/or inpatient admissions within previous 6 months(1)(7)

A. There are numerous measurement tools used to assess for frailty. Some of the more commonly used scales (with score indicating
frailty in parentheses) include the following: Frailty Phenotype (3 or higher), 40-item Frailty Index (0.25 or higher), Study of
Osteoporotic Fracture Index (2 or higher), Edmonton Frail Scale (8 or higher), FRAIL Scale (3 or higher), Clinical Frailty Scale (5 or
higher), and Tilburg Frailty Indicator (5 or higher).(4)
B. Frailty may be described as a phenotype or as an accumulation of health deficits. The Fried phenotype delineates a clinical
syndrome resulting from altered metabolism coupled with abnormal stress responses.(5) This model includes 5 characteristic
features: exhaustion (energy level), weakness (hand grip strength), slowness (gait speed), physical inactivity (falls), and weight loss.
(5)(6) The presence of 3 or more of these deficits indicates the presence of frailty.(5)(6) Frailty as deficit accumulation considers
findings in multiple domains (eg, cognitive, physical, nutritional, laboratory) and high-risk comorbidities.(5)(6) In this model, the
degree of frailty is quantified by the number of indicative items present.(5)

system_template.override_body: Item: Operative Status Criteria. Scope: determine whether inpatient is the appropriate operative status for the requested abdominal hysterectomy as an intake decision only. Use only the Operative Status Criteria section plus patient-specific source documentation. Do not evaluate postoperative recovery milestones, discharge planning, or extended-stay items as independent approval criteria. Guideline anchor: Goal Length of Stay is 2 days postoperative and operative status is Inpatient. CMS inpatient-only language in the rationale is supporting context for Medicare review but does not replace the need for chart-supported operative context. Required review steps: 1. Confirm the planned or requested procedure is abdominal hysterectomy rather than laparoscopic-only, vaginal-only, or another route. 2. Look for explicit admission, surgical booking, operative planning, pre-op, surgeon, anesthesia, or hospital documentation that the case is intended for inpatient hospital status. 3. Look for chart-supported features consistent with inpatient open abdominal surgery context, such as open laparotomy approach, expected inpatient postprocedure management, significant comorbidity burden, oncologic or complex gynecologic indication, hemorrhage or emergent setting, or other documented clinical factors making inpatient operative status appropriate. 4. Exclude nonclinical evidence such as UR/UM forms, authorization checklists, copied guideline text, fax headers, and printed-at dates. Decision rules: level_of_care is INPATIENT only when the chart affirmatively supports inpatient operative status for this abdominal hysterectomy request. level_of_care is OBSERVATION only when the chart affirmatively supports a lower hospital status or clearly describes a setting inconsistent with inpatient abdominal hysterectomy. level_of_care is NEEDS_REVIEW when the procedure route, admission intent, or level-of-care support is unclear or conflicting. status is MET only when level_of_care is INPATIENT. status is NOT_MET when chart evidence affirmatively supports OBSERVATION or another non-inpatient posture. status is MISSING_INFORMATION when level_of_care cannot be resolved confidently. Precision-first instructions: do not assume inpatient status from diagnosis alone, from the existence of surgery alone, or from generic references to hysterectomy. Do not use postoperative day tables to justify intake status. Require affirmative source-record evidence for inpatient designation and explain what evidence did or did not support that conclusion.
